questions.name: Multi-factor authentication
questions.text: Is multi-factor authentication (MFA) required for email, remote access, and admin accounts?

options.label: Yes, for all users and all of these systems
For admins and remote access, but not all users
Only on a few accounts or optional
No MFA anywhere

remediation.action: Turn on MFA for every user's email and remote access, starting with admin accounts.
remediation.why: Stolen passwords are the most common way attackers get in. MFA stops most of those attempts even when the password is known.

questions.name: Admin rights
questions.text: Do everyday user accounts have administrator rights on their computers?

options.label: No, admin rights are limited to IT staff
A few users have them for a documented reason
Many users have admin rights
Everyone is an administrator

remediation.action: Remove local admin rights from everyday accounts and give IT separate admin logins.
remediation.why: When a user with admin rights clicks a malicious link, the attacker gets full control of the computer.

questions.name: Account offboarding
questions.text: When an employee leaves, how quickly are their accounts disabled?

options.label: Same day, using a written offboarding checklist
Within a week
Eventually, when someone remembers
Accounts are rarely or never disabled

remediation.action: Create an offboarding checklist that disables all accounts on the employee's last day, and review active accounts quarterly.
remediation.why: Former employees' accounts are an open door. Nobody notices when they're misused.

questions.name: Password management
questions.text: Do staff use unique passwords stored in a password manager?

options.label: Yes, a company password manager is provided and used
Encouraged, but not provided or enforced
Passwords are often shared or reused
Shared passwords are written down or kept in spreadsheets

remediation.action: Roll out a company password manager and require unique passwords for every system.
remediation.why: Reused or shared passwords mean one breach anywhere unlocks accounts everywhere.

questions.name: Backup frequency
questions.text: How often is critical business data backed up?

options.label: Automatically, at least daily
Weekly
Monthly or manually when someone remembers
No regular backups

remediation.action: Set up automatic daily backups of all critical systems and shared files.
remediation.why: Without recent backups, ransomware or a failed drive can mean permanent loss of records and days of downtime.

questions.name: Offline / immutable backups
questions.text: Is at least one backup copy kept offline or immutable (can't be changed or deleted)?

options.label: Yes, an offline or immutable copy is kept separate from the network
Cloud backup only, with version history
Backups sit on the same network as the data
No separate backup copy

remediation.action: Keep at least one backup copy offline or in immutable cloud storage that ordinary accounts can't delete.
remediation.why: Ransomware deliberately looks for connected backups and encrypts them too. A separate copy is what makes recovery possible.

questions.name: Restore testing
questions.text: Has restoring from backup been tested?

options.label: Yes, a full restore is tested at least twice a year
Tested once in the last year
Never formally tested
We don't know if restores would work

remediation.action: Run a test restore of one critical system every six months and record how long it takes.
remediation.why: Many businesses only discover their backups are broken in the middle of an emergency.

questions.name: Software updates
questions.text: How are operating system and software updates installed?

options.label: Automatically, and critical updates within 14 days
Monthly, by IT
Users install updates when they choose to
Updates aren't managed

remediation.action: Turn on automatic updates for all computers and apply critical security patches within 14 days.
remediation.why: Attackers exploit known vulnerabilities within days of a patch being released. Unpatched systems are the easiest targets.

questions.name: End-of-life software
questions.text: Is any unsupported (end-of-life) software or operating system still in use?

options.label: No, everything is still supported by its vendor
One or two systems, with a replacement planned
Several systems, with no replacement plan
We don't know

remediation.action: Identify all end-of-life systems and budget to replace or isolate them within the next year.
remediation.why: Unsupported software no longer receives security fixes, so every new vulnerability stays open permanently.

questions.name: Asset inventory
questions.text: Is there an up-to-date inventory of company devices and software?

options.label: Yes, complete and reviewed at least quarterly
Partial or updated once a year
Outdated list
No inventory

remediation.action: Build a simple inventory of every device and key application, with its owner, and review it quarterly.
remediation.why: You can't patch, back up, or protect what you don't know you have.

questions.name: Endpoint protection
questions.text: Do all computers run centrally managed antivirus or endpoint protection?

options.label: Yes, managed and monitored on every device
Installed everywhere, but not monitored
Only on some devices
No endpoint protection

remediation.action: Deploy managed endpoint protection on every device, with alerts sent to IT or your service provider.
remediation.why: Endpoint protection catches and blocks most common malware before it spreads.

questions.name: Security training
questions.text: How often do employees receive security awareness training?

options.label: At onboarding and at least once a year
At onboarding only
Occasionally, with no schedule
Never

remediation.action: Require short security training for every new hire and an annual refresher for all staff.
remediation.why: Most breaches start with a person being tricked. Trained staff spot and report attacks earlier.

questions.name: Phishing simulations
questions.text: Does the company run phishing simulation exercises?

options.label: Yes, at least quarterly, with results tracked
Once or twice a year
Tried once
Never

remediation.action: Run quarterly phishing simulations and track the click and report rates over time.
remediation.why: Practice makes phishing recognition a habit, and the results show where extra training is needed.

questions.name: Incident reporting channel
questions.text: Do employees know exactly how to report a suspicious email or security issue?

options.label: Yes, there's a report button or address and staff use it
There's a process, but not everyone knows it
People tell whoever they happen to think of
No reporting process

remediation.action: Set up one clear reporting channel, such as a report-phishing button or a security email address, and announce it to all staff.
remediation.why: Fast reporting shortens how long an attacker has before they're stopped.

questions.name: Incident response plan
questions.text: Is there a written incident response plan?

options.label: Yes, and it's been practiced in the last year
Written, but never practiced
Informal: people would figure it out
No plan

remediation.action: Write a two-page incident response plan covering who decides, who to call, and first steps, then walk through it once a year.
remediation.why: Decisions made calmly in advance are faster and better than decisions made mid-crisis.

questions.name: Emergency contacts
questions.text: Are emergency contacts documented (IT provider, cyber insurer, legal counsel)?

options.label: Yes, documented and stored where they can be reached offline
Partly documented
Known only by one or two people
Not documented

remediation.action: Keep a printed and offline list of emergency contacts: IT support, cyber insurer, legal counsel, and key vendors.
remediation.why: During an attack, email and shared drives may be unavailable exactly when the contacts are needed.

questions.name: Device encryption
questions.text: Are laptops and mobile devices encrypted?

options.label: Yes, all devices, with encryption enforced
Most devices
Some devices
None, or we don't know

remediation.action: Turn on built-in full-disk encryption (BitLocker or FileVault) on every laptop and enforce it centrally.
remediation.why: A lost or stolen laptop without encryption is a data breach. With encryption, it's just a lost device.

questions.name: Sensitive data access
questions.text: Is access to sensitive data (customer, financial, HR) limited to the people who need it?

options.label: Yes, role-based access that is reviewed regularly
Mostly restricted, but rarely reviewed
Loosely restricted, so many people can access it
Everyone can access everything

remediation.action: Restrict sensitive folders and systems to the roles that need them, and review who has access twice a year.
remediation.why: Limiting access reduces how much data one compromised account or careless mistake can expose.
